title: Developer Experience SDK Quickstarts, API Examples & Top Issues Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This playbook defines the standards, operating procedures, and canonical artifacts for Developer Experience (DevEx) documentation focused on: SDK guides, quickstarts and templates, API examples, docs site operating procedures, and the top support issues + canonical fixes. It is intended for the Docs, SDK, and DevEx engineers responsible for producing and maintaining user-facing developer documentation and first-line support content.

Goals
- Provide fast, consistent onboarding for developers using Redwood APIs and SDKs.
- Reduce support load by surfacing canonical fixes and easily discoverable troubleshooting guidance.
- Maintain a single source of truth for SDK patterns, code examples, and quickstarts.
- Ensure docs updates follow release and quality check processes so examples remain runnable.

Scope
- SDK guides (Python, TypeScript/Node, Go, Java) and idiomatic patterns for generation, chat, embeddings, and streaming.
- Quickstarts and project templates for common integration patterns (serverless, backend inference, embeddings search, sidecar usage).
- API examples (curl and SDK snippets) including function/tool-calling and streaming clients.
- Docs site operating procedures: publishing workflow, content review, link checks, and telemetry.
- Top support issues: triage steps, root-cause checklists, and canonical fixes.

Owners and Roles
- Primary owner: DevEx Docs Team (engineering) — contact: devex-docs@redwood.ai
- SDK maintainers: individual SDK teams (see per-language OWNER file).
- Support liaison: Customer Success triage lead for developer issues.
- Reviewers: product engineering and security for any API or auth changes.

Structure and Conventions
1) File and page naming
  - Short, dashed names: e.g. developer-experience-sdk-quickstarts-2026.json
  - Template files go under quickstarts-and-templates/ with matching example repos in Github (link in frontmatter).
2) Example code rules
  - All code blocks must be executable (where feasible).
  - Include pinned SDK versions and minimal requirements in a code snippet block.
  - Keep examples < 60 LOC for quickstarts; link to full example repo for larger samples.
3) Headings and modular sections
  - Use the canonical headings: Overview, Requirements, Quickstart, Code, Troubleshooting, Next steps.
  - Include a one-line purpose at the top of each doc.

Docs Site Operating Procedures
- Branching and publishing
  1. Draft in docs-site branch; add reviewer(s) and label 'doc-review'.
  2. Run link-check, spell-check, and example-runner CI (see docs-site/ci).
  3. After approvals, merge to main and tag release with docs version.
- Release cadence
  - Hotfixes: as-needed (critical breaking examples or security-related changes).
  - Regular updates: aligned with SDK releases and monthly content sprints.
- Monitoring and telemetry
  - Track: pageviews, search failure rate (no-click outcomes), and support ticket references per doc.
  - Weekly dashboard: top 20 pages by traffic and top 10 search terms leading to support.

SDK Guides (Authoring Checklist)
- Purpose and audience: state whether the guide is for quick onboarding, advanced usage, or migration.
- Requirements: OS, SDK version, API key scope, environment variables.
- Short runnable example: a 5–15 line snippet demonstrating common success path.
- Error handling section: common error codes, retry recommendations, idempotency notes.
- Security notes: credential handling, token rotation, scopes required.

Quickstarts and Templates
- Canonical quickstarts:
  - embeddings-search-quickstart: indexing local dataset -> generate embeddings -> simple search API
  - chat-bot-quickstart: integrating streaming responses with a minimal frontend
  - batch-generation-quickstart: working with Redwood Dedicated for throughput
- Templates must include:
  - README with step-by-step run instructions
  - example.env with required env vars and a minimal .gitignore rules
  - CI workflow to validate the quickstart can run headlessly (GitHub Actions).

API Examples (Best Practices)
- Provide both curl and SDK snippets for each endpoint: generation, chat, embeddings, reranking.
- Indicate the expected response schema and common fields.
- For streaming examples include the client-side processing loop pseudocode and how to handle partial events.

Top Support Issues & Canonical Fixes
- Problem: Auth error: "401 api_key_invalid"
  - First-check: confirm API_KEY env var is present and not expired.
  - Canonical fix: regenerate key in Console -> re-run quickstart with export REDWOOD_API_KEY=...
  - Notes: include curl example showing header: -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY"
- Problem: Streaming payload truncation or unexpected EOF
  - First-check: client network/proxy terminating connections; verify keep-alive.
  - Canonical fix: add Retry-After/backoff and enable SDK's streaming-reconnect option (code snippet below).
- Problem: Mismatch between local SDK version and hosted API (schema errors)
  - First-check: run sdk --version and inspect response schema in curl example.
  - Canonical fix: pin SDK to supported version and add compatibility note in the quickstart.

Procedures: triage and escalate
1) Triage (support engineer)
  - Reproduce with canonical quickstart in a clean environment.
  - Capture logs, request IDs, timestamps, and SDK version.
  - If reproducible, attach failing request/response (redact PII) and escalate to SDK owner.
2) Severity matrix
  - Sev1: production-facing breaking API change or docs causing data loss -> page the oncall and create incident.
  - Sev2: major developer workflow blocked (quickstart broken) -> 24h fix SLA.
  - Sev3: minor doc clarity or cosmetic issues -> tracked in next docs sprint.

Canonical Fix Examples (snippets)
- Curl auth example:
  curl -sS -X POST \
    https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"input":"Hello","model":"redwood-1.2"}'

- Node streaming reconnect pseudocode:
  const client = new RedwoodStreamingClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, reconnect: true, reconnectBackoffMs: 1000 });
  client.on('data', (chunk) => { process.stdout.write(chunk); });
  client.on('error', (err) => { console.error('stream error', err); });

Quality Gates and Review Checklist
- Docs changes must pass the docs CI (link-checker, example-runner).
- Security review required when examples add new scopes or change auth flows.
- SDK examples must be smoke-tested on supported runtimes (Node 18+, Python 3.10+).

Metrics and KPIs
- Objective: reduce developer friction and support load.
- Leading indicators: decreased "how-to" tickets per 1k API calls; increased quickstart-run success rate in CI.
- Targets: reduce repeat support incidents tied to docs by 40% within 6 months of playbook adoption.

Appendix: Quickstart Template (minimal)
- README excerpt:
  # Quickstart: embeddings-search
  Purpose: index a small dataset and run a simple vector search against Redwood embeddings.
  Requirements: Node 18+, REDWOOD_API_KEY
  Steps:
    1. npm install
    2. export REDWOOD_API_KEY=...
    3. node index.js
- index.js excerpt:
  const { RedwoodClient } = require('@redwood/sdk');
  const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
  async function main(){
    const embed = await client.embeddings.create({ model: 'embed-1.0', input: ['hello world'] });
    console.log(embed.data[0].embedding.length);
  }
  main();

Related pages and links

- SDK repo indexing: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-examples
- Support escalation playbook: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/escalation-playbook

Change log
- 2026-01-12: initial published draft by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-02-20: added top support issues and canonical fixes; updated release cadence notes.

If you are updating code examples: always run the example-runner locally and add a test case to the sdk-examples repo before submitting the PR.
